title: Strong Kaomoji ᕦ(ò_óˇ)ᕤ: Copy & Paste Flex and Proud Faces
meta_description: Copy and paste strong kaomoji: flexing arms like ᕦ(ò_óˇ)ᕤ and ᕙ(⇀‸↼‶)ᕗ, determined faces like (ง •̀_•́)ง, proud (￣^￣) faces and you-got-this cheers.
hero_tagline: Text faces flexing their biceps, setting their jaw or puffing out their chest with pride. Tap one and it lands on your clipboard.
intro: Most strong kaomoji are built on one trick: the Canadian Syllabics letters ᕦ and ᕤ, or ᕙ and ᕗ, curl up on each side of the face like an arm bent to show a bicep. The face in the middle sets the mood, so ò_ó with slanted brows looks fierce while ᐛ grins. Determined faces swap the flex for fists raised in a boxing guard, and proud faces tilt the nose up with ￣^￣. People post them after a gym session, before an exam, or to tell a friend they can handle what is coming. Each one is ordinary Unicode text, so it pastes into any field that accepts Unicode text.

sections.label: Flexing Arms
sections.intro: The flex faces people search for most. ᕦ ᕤ and ᕙ ᕗ are the raised arms, and ˇ or ‶ adds a bead of effort.

sections.label: Determined
sections.intro: Fists up and eyebrows down. ง is a Thai letter whose hook reads as a curled fist, and •̀ •́ are eyes with a stern accent mark over them.

sections.label: Proud
sections.intro: ￣^￣ is a turned-up nose, the text version of puffing out your chest. Use these after a win, big or small.

sections.label: You Got This
sections.h2: You Got This Kaomoji to Cheer Someone On
sections.intro: Faces to send someone else before their big day. The ✧ sparkles and ♪ notes make them read as encouragement rather than bragging.

faq.q: What are the arms in ᕦ(ò_óˇ)ᕤ made of?
faq.a: They are letters from the Unified Canadian Aboriginal Syllabics block, which is used to write Inuktitut and Cree. ᕦ and ᕤ happen to curl like a flexed arm, so kaomoji makers borrowed them. A device without a font for the block shows a box in place of the arms.
It is a face holding its fists up in a fighting stance. People use it to say they are ready to take something on, such as a deadline, a workout or a boss fight in a game.

faq.q: What does ganbatte mean next to a kaomoji?
faq.a: Ganbatte (頑張って) is Japanese for "do your best" or "hang in there". It is often paired with a determined face to cheer someone on before a test or a match.
